title: Substitute Teaching in the Atlanta Area School for the Deaf
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Dan Meyer recounts guest-teaching a geometry lesson on prisms to deaf students in Atlanta, working through an ASL interpreter. The experience gives him a sharper statement of an old teaching problem: what students know, what they can communicate about it, and what the teacher understands of that communication are three different sets that only partly overlap. He corrects his own assumptions about ASL, which is a separate language with its own grammar and visual nuance, and notes that language deprivation leaves many deaf students better able to express mathematical thinking in ASL than in written English. His move is to generalize: this is not an exotic situation but the condition under which everyone teaches. The practical stance he models is to value student ideas first, then connect them to the shared mathematical definition and why it is useful.
points: What students know, what they can express, and what the teacher grasps of that expression are different sets that only partly overlap.
ASL is a distinct language with multidimensional, visual features, and some math ideas may be explained more clearly in it than in English.
Language deprivation means written English can understate what deaf students actually think about a concept.
Teachers can honor student thinking about a concept while still introducing the conventional mathematical definition and showing what it makes possible.
All classrooms are cross-language to some degree, so there is always more in a student's mind than the teacher sees or hears.
quotes: I had also assumed that ASL was communicated through hands alone—that the static pictures of signs you may have seen are the entire meaning of the word one communicates in ASL. Lara clarified, however, that ASL is communicated through hands moving multidimensionally through space, at different speeds, attached to a person with a face making expressions, the sum of which can endow communication in ASL more nuance and meaning than the same words in spoken English.

Lara told me that deaf kids often suffer from language deprivation since many deaf children are not exposed to an accessible language early in life. While hearing babies are constantly absorbing and learning language just by existing in a world full of spoken words, deaf babies and children often don’t receive the same resources, informally or even formally.

Mathematics is a discipline that delights in its nuances and distinctions. (It isn’t just a triangle, it’s an obtuse triangle. It isn’t just a number, it’s a rational number.) And my students and I were going to have very different languages for communicating nuance and distinction.

One consequence of that deprivation is that my deaf students could more accurately express their thinking about prisms in ASL, a language I don’t understand, than they could in written English, a language I do understand. So the students would express their ideas in ASL to their interpreter who would express them verbally to me—a game of telephone with everyone using different languages and having different kinds of knowledge about the subject they're trying to discuss.

I said throughout the lesson, as much to remind myself as to communicate it to students, "Other mathematicians have defined prisms differently from you folks, but your mind and your eyes are working together to produce some really interesting thinking.

We're always teaching students whose ideas about mathematics—the patterns they're noticing, their estimations about quantities and shapes, etc.—outstrip their ability to express them. It's perhaps more obvious when students haven’t received adequate instruction in written English or when their primary language is different from ours. But I'm grateful for the reminder that there is always more going on in a student's mind than meets our eyes or ears.
